sweeps.summary: Short answer: for C1 as stated, it has not been done before. I found no work that lengthens targeted vowel nuclei in HUMAN recordings, matches the added duration exactly against uniform slowing, sweeps k, and scores the gap with several ASR families. The field splits in two. (1) Rate-robustness benchmarks (Speech Robust Bench, SPECOM 2024 Whisper benchmark, EURASIP JASMP 2026, the SLAM-ASR evaluation, the AIx Speed pilot) apply only uniform tempo or stretch changes. (2) Local-lengthening work either injects prolongations with no global arm (ASTER, Mujtaba NAACL 2024, both already cited; Kruspe 2015 for training) or aims to improve intelligibility or normalise pathological rhythm. The closest items are already cited, but may be under-credited. Tuttosi SSW 2025 and arXiv 2603.30032 each contain a Whisper-ASR arm on SYNTHETIC TTS in which global slowing beats targeted stretching for the machine. That is the same direction as C1, but ratio-matched rather than duration-matched, with one model and one factor. The manuscript should credit these ASR arms explicitly, not only the human-listener results. El Hajal 2025 (ICASSP and Interspeech versions) compares global vs syllable-level rhythm conversion of human dysarthric speech with Whisper and finds global as good or better. The authors blame local-arm artifacts informally, which foreshadows C2 but never measures artifact damage. AIx Speed (2023) is an uncited counterpoint: at matched average speed on LibriSpeech, an ASR-optimised non-uniform speed-up has LOWER wav2vec2 WER than uniform. C1 should therefore be framed as specific to lengthening targeted vowel nuclei, not as 'local is always worse'. None of these pre-empts C2 to C5. Limits: the session's web-search budget ran out near the end, and Xiong 2019 plus the two global-only benchmarks were judged from abstracts only.

candidates.t: You Sound a Little Tense: L2 Tailored Clear TTS Using Durational Vowel Properties (plus the same Whisper result in Tuttosi's PhD thesis 'I Know You're Listening: Adaptive Voice for HRI', arXiv 2506.15107, Table 5.8)
candidates.v: Tuttosi, Yeung, Wang, Aucouturier, Lim; 2025; ISCA SSW 2025 (arXiv 2506.23367); thesis SFU 2025
candidates.why: Same direction as C1 for an ASR (targeted lengthening is worse for Whisper than uniform slowing), but: synthetic TTS voice, not human; ratio-matched, not added-duration matched (the global arm gets much more added time); a single Whisper model; no stretch-factor sweep; durations come from the TTS, not a TSM engine, so there is no artifact control. If the manuscript credits Tuttosi 2025 only for the human-listener finding, it under-credits this Whisper arm and should say so explicitly.

candidates.t: Covertly improving intelligibility with data-driven adaptations of speech timing
candidates.v: Tuttosi, Lim, Yeung, Wang, Aucouturier; 2026; arXiv 2603.30032
candidates.why: Directly compares targeted vs global slowing on an ASR and finds global better for the machine. That is the qualitative core of C1, but only on synthetic speech, ratio-matched (not added-duration matched), with one Whisper model and one factor, and no TSM-artifact control. C1's novelty rests on human recordings, exact added-duration matching, the k sweep and multiple model families. The manuscript should credit Study 3c explicitly, not only the listener studies.

candidates.t: Unsupervised Rhythm and Voice Conversion of Dysarthric to Healthy Speech for ASR (ICASSP 2025) and Unsupervised Rhythm and Voice Conversion to Improve ASR on Dysarthric Speech (Interspeech 2025)
candidates.v: El Hajal, Hermann, Kulkarni / Hovsepyan, Magimai-Doss; 2025; ICASSP 2025 (arXiv 2501.10256) and Interspeech 2025 (arXiv 2506.01618)
candidates.why: The only human-speech local-vs-global duration comparison scored by ASR (Whisper) that I found. It misses C1's essentials: it compresses and normalises pathological speech rather than adding duration; allocation is not targeted to vowel nuclei; there is no exact added-duration match and no k sweep; both arms go through a unit vocoder. Its informal note that local-arm artifacts drive the gap foreshadows C2, but it never measures artifact damage (no round-trip). If the manuscript cites only one of the two versions, the global-vs-fine-grained comparison appears in both and should be acknowledged.

candidates.t: AIx Speed: Playback Speed Optimization Using Listening Comprehension of Speech Recognition Models
candidates.v: Kawamura, Rekimoto; 2023; Augmented Humans (AHs '23), ACM (arXiv 2403.02938)
candidates.why: It shares a key ingredient of C1's design: non-uniform vs uniform time-scaling of human speech at matched overall duration, scored by ASR WER. But it speeds up instead of lengthening, the ASR itself picks the allocation (benign by construction), there is no vowel targeting and no artifact control. Its finding (well-chosen local changes hurt less than uniform ones) is a useful counterpoint: C1 should be scoped to lengthening targeted vowel nuclei, not to any non-uniform allocation.

candidates.t: Phonetic Analysis of Dysarthric Speech Tempo and Applications to Robust Personalised Dysarthric Speech Recognition
candidates.v: Xiong, Barker, Christensen; 2019; ICASSP 2019, pp. 5836-5840
candidates.why: Background for phone-selective duration changes of human speech evaluated by ASR. The goal is normalisation or augmentation for a hybrid system; it does not test targeted lengthening against a duration-matched uniform slowing on modern end-to-end models. Only the abstract and snippets were available; the full text was paywalled.

candidates.t: Training phoneme models for singing with 'songified' speech data
candidates.v: Kruspe; 2015; ISMIR 2015
candidates.why: Early precedent for alignment-based, vowel-only lengthening of human speech fed to a recogniser, but only as training augmentation. There is no uniform-slowing arm, no duration matching and no test-time robustness comparison. Worth a background cite for the manipulation itself.

candidates.t: Performance evaluation of SLAM-ASR: The Good, the Bad, the Ugly, and the Way Forward
candidates.v: Kumar et al. (Idiap/Uniphore); 2024; arXiv 2411.03866
candidates.why: Global-only tempo robustness; no local arm and no duration matching. Relevant as recent evidence that uniform slowing alone degrades modern ASR, which is the baseline arm of C1. Known from the abstract and snippets only.

candidates.t: Speech recognition in adverse conditions: synthetic transformations and real environmental noise
candidates.v: EURASIP Journal on Audio, Speech, and Music Processing, 2026 (article 13636-026-00458-1)
candidates.why: Uniform time-stretch only: no local or targeted arm, no duration-matched contrast and no TSM artifact audit. Background alongside Speech Robust Bench (already cited).

sweeps.summary: Short answer to the user: from the disfluency and prolongation side, no. Nothing I found already does the paper's core comparison. I searched 2010 to 2026 across web search, arXiv, ACL Anthology and ISCA, and opened the method sections of the closest hits. No stuttering or dysfluency simulation work compares a local prolongation of human speech against a global slowdown of exactly the same added duration. None checks per arm how much of the WER damage comes from the time-stretch engine itself (C2's round trip). There is also no Rubber Band vs phase vocoder comparison for this purpose. C3 to C5 are not touched by this literature. Closest work: Mujtaba et al. NAACL 2024, which the paper already cites. It uses the same English setup as the paper's English arm: LibriSpeech test-clean, wav2vec2 CTC forced alignment, Whisper and wav2vec2. It stretches 1 to 3 word onsets 5 to 25x and reports large WER increases, so 'local lengthening raises WER' on this setup is already known. The paper should credit that explicitly and present its novelty as the duration-matched global control, the dose curve over k, and the artifact audit. El Hajal et al. 2025 (also cited) compares global vs fine-grained time-stretching on dysarthric ASR and blames artifacts for the fine-grained loss. Its direction is the reverse (shortening slow dysarthric speech), its arms are not exactly duration-matched, and it has no round-trip control, so it is partial at most and deserves a more specific citation. The rest (LibriStutter, VCTK++ with WSOLA, VCTK-Stutter/YOLO-Stutter, Stutter-Solver, LLM-Dys, Stutter-TTS, DisSpeech, the Indonesian TTS work) use stretching or TTS duration control to train dysfluency detectors or ASR. They never contrast with a matched global slowdown. Two useful context points: (1) the Berkeley group reports that waveform-edited dysfluencies sound much less natural (MOS 2.22 vs 4.13) and moved to TTS instead of measuring artifacts; (2) real-speech studies (Lea et al. CHI 2023; 2026 dual-reference benchmark) find that natural prolongations barely affect WER. Both support the paper's motivation for an artifact control. Caveat: Semantic Scholar was rate-limited, so coverage relied on web search, the arXiv API and direct PDF reads.

candidates.t: Lost in Transcription: Identifying and Quantifying the Accuracy Biases of Automatic Speech Recognition Systems Against Disfluent Speech
candidates.v: Mujtaba, Mahapatra, Arney, Yaruss, Gerlach-Houck, Herring, Bin; 2024; NAACL 2024 (arXiv 2405.06150)
candidates.why: Same English substrate as the paper's English arm (LibriSpeech test-clean, forced alignment, wav2vec2 and Whisper) and already shows that locally lengthening a few segments of human speech raises WER sharply. It misses the essential part of C1: there is no global-slowing arm, no duration matching, no vowel/stress targeting, no dose curve over k, and no artifact control (C2). Pre-empts more than a 'disfluency bias' credit: the paper should say explicitly that local lengthening hurting WER on LibriSpeech with these model families is known, and that its contribution is the matched global contrast plus artifact audit. Also note its extreme factors (5 to 25x) vs the paper's k in {2,4,6}.

candidates.t: Unsupervised Rhythm and Voice Conversion to Improve ASR on Dysarthric Speech
candidates.v: El Hajal, Hermann, Hovsepyan, Magimai.-Doss; 2025; Interspeech 2025 (arXiv 2506.01618); companion: El Hajal et al. 2025, arXiv 2501.10256
candidates.why: A direct global-vs-local time-stretch comparison on ASR WER, with an artifact explanation for the local arm's loss. But the direction is the reverse (shortening pathological speech toward typical rate, not adding lengthening to typical speech), arms are not constructed as exactly duration-matched, processing is in discrete SSL units plus a vocoder, and there is no artifact-isolating check like the round trip. Note that its artifact story runs opposite to the paper's C2 finding (here local processing is the arm that artifacts hurt). Worth citing for this global-vs-fine-grained result, not only as 'rhythm conversion'.

candidates.t: FluentNet: End-to-End Detection of Stuttered Speech Disfluencies With Deep Learning (introduces LibriStutter)
candidates.v: Kourkounakis, Hajavi, Etemad; 2021; IEEE/ACM TASLP (arXiv 2009.11394)
candidates.why: Shares only the ingredient of stretching a sub-word segment of human read speech. No ASR WER measurement, no global-slowing control, no duration matching, no TSM artifact audit. The authors' need for pitch correction does show that their stretch was not clean, which fits the motivation for C2.

candidates.t: Unconstrained Dysfluency Modeling for Dysfluent Speech Transcription and Detection (VCTK++)
candidates.v: Lian, Feng, Farooqi, Li, Kashyap, Cho, Wu, Netzorg, Li, Anumanchipalli; 2023; IEEE ASRU 2023 (arXiv 2312.12810)
candidates.why: Targeted phoneme lengthening of human speech with a named TSM (WSOLA) at forced-aligned positions, but the purpose is dysfluency detection and transcription training. It does not compare against global slowing at matched duration and does not measure or control TSM artifacts.

candidates.t: YOLO-Stutter: End-to-end Region-Wise Speech Dysfluency Detection (VCTK-Stutter vs VCTK-TTS)
candidates.v: Zhou, Lian, et al.; 2024; Interspeech 2024 (arXiv 2408.15297); follow-ups Stutter-Solver (arXiv 2409.09621) and LLM-Dys (Interspeech 2025, arXiv 2505.22029)
candidates.why: This line of work recognizes that waveform-level lengthening creates unnatural artifacts. It responds by moving to TTS or articulatory synthesis, not by measuring how much of an ASR effect is artifact. There is no ASR WER, no global control, and no per-arm artifact measurement. It is background for C2, not a pre-emption.

candidates.t: From User Perceptions to Technical Improvement: Enabling People Who Stutter to Better Use Speech Recognition
candidates.v: Lea, Huang, Narain, Tooley, Yee, Tran, Georgiou, Bigham, Findlater; 2023; CHI 2023 (arXiv 2302.09044)
candidates.why: Natural prolongations barely hurt ASR, while synthetically stretched ones hurt it a lot (Mujtaba 2024: 0.32 to 0.55 WER). That contrast points to stretch artifacts or extreme factors as a confound in synthetic-prolongation studies, which supports the need for C2. No duration-matched manipulation, no global control.

candidates.t: The Effectiveness of Time Stretching for Enhancing Dysarthric Speech for Improved Dysarthric Speech Recognition
candidates.v: Prananta, Halpern, Feng, Scharenborg; 2022; Interspeech 2022 (arXiv 2201.04908)
candidates.why: Global phase-vocoder stretching only, used as enhancement. No local arm, no duration-matched contrast, no artifact audit. Background for the global arm and for phase-vocoder use in ASR pipelines.

sweeps.summary: Nothing I found pre-empts C2 or C3. No paper uses a stretch-and-restore round trip at unchanged duration to measure a TSM engine's artifact-only ASR damage separately per condition. No paper shows that a TSM engine biases a local-vs-global ASR comparison, or ties that bias to an artifact imbalance between arms. Closest precedents: (1) Reinisch 2016, which resynthesized unmanipulated sentences by speeding them up and slowing them down again so every condition carried the same PSOLA artifacts. That is a round-trip control, but only as an equalizer, with human listeners and no measurement. The paper should cite it and frame its own contribution as turning the round trip into a per-arm diagnostic for ASR plus an engine comparison. (2) Speech-coding compress/expand cascades (Makhoul & El-Jaroudi 1986; Philips patent 2001), which document the artifacts left after a TSM round trip. (3) Paulus et al. 2019, which compares local (VocALign) and global (WSOLA) retiming of natural speech with a different engine in each arm and no artifact control: an uncontrolled instance of the confound the paper diagnoses. STSM-FiLM 2025 uses ASR WER to rank TSM engines, but its WER mixes duration change with artifacts. Prananta 2022 applies librosa's phase vocoder in an ASR duration study without any artifact control. On the already-cited Tuttosi et al. 2026 (arXiv 2603.30032), I read the PDF, and it does not pre-empt more than credited. Its conditions come straight from Matcha-TTS duration control, so no TSM engine was involved. Stretch-everywhere (1.2x whole phrase) and stretch-every-target (1.2x on targets) are ratio-matched, not duration-matched. For Whisper, stretch-everywhere lowered WER the most, which is directionally consistent with C1, and the paper may want to note that. Its Study 1 used CLEESE, a phase vocoder, for local rate changes. Iwamoto 2022 (cited) isolates an artifact-only WER component for speech enhancement, which is a conceptual analog of C2 in another domain; the current credit is adequate. Coverage limits: the session's shared web-search budget ran out after these queries, Semantic Scholar returned rate limits, and IEEE Xplore pages were not fetchable. An IEEE-only ICASSP or TASLP paper could therefore have been missed, though arXiv API and OpenAlex keyword sweeps found nothing further.

candidates.t: Natural fast speech is perceived as faster than linearly time-compressed speech
candidates.v: E. Reinisch, 2016, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 78
candidates.why: This is the clearest precedent I found for the stretch-and-restore idea: a TSM round trip at unchanged duration used as an artifact control. It is used only to equalize processing across conditions. It never measures artifact damage, per arm or otherwise. The listeners are human, not ASR, only PSOLA is used, and there is no engine comparison or evidence that an engine biases a contrast. C2's novelty should be framed as turning the round trip into a per-arm artifact-damage measurement for ASR, and this paper should be cited.

candidates.t: Talker intelligibility and listening effort with temporally modified speech
candidates.v: M. Paulus, V. Hazan, P. Adank, 2019, Interspeech
candidates.why: It compares local and global rate changes on human speech, but with human listeners, no duration matching, and a different engine in each arm (VocALign vs WSOLA). There is no round-trip or other artifact control. It is a published example of the arm-specific engine confound that C2/C3 diagnose, and the authors themselves suspect processing distortion. It does not do C1's ASR comparison at matched duration.

candidates.t: STSM-FiLM: A FiLM-Conditioned Neural Architecture for Time-Scale Modification of Speech
candidates.v: D. A. M. G. Wisnu, R. E. Zezario, S. Rini, F.-R. Li, Y.-T. Peng, H.-M. Wang, Y. Tsao, 2025, arXiv 2510.02672
candidates.why: It shares one ingredient: ASR WER used to rank TSM engines by damage. Its WER is measured on stretched speech, so duration change and artifacts are confounded. There is no round trip at unchanged duration, no local vs global arms, and no phase-vocoder baseline or bias analysis (I checked the HTML).

candidates.t: The Effectiveness of Time Stretching for Enhancing Dysarthric Speech for Improved Dysarthric Speech Recognition
candidates.v: L. Prananta, B. M. Halpern, S. Feng, O. Scharenborg, 2022, Interspeech (arXiv 2201.04908)
candidates.why: Background only. It shows librosa's default phase vocoder in practice for ASR duration experiments, with no artifact control (I read the PDF). This is exactly the practice C2 warns about. It has no round trip, no local arm and no engine comparison.

candidates.t: Time-scale modification of signals (compress before coding, reciprocal expand after decoding), US Patent 7412379; builds on Makhoul & El-Jaroudi, 'Time-scale modification in medium to low rate speech coding', ICASSP 1986
candidates.v: R. Taori, A. J. Gerrits, D. Burazerovic (Philips), priority 2001; Makhoul & El-Jaroudi 1986, ICASSP
candidates.why: An old precedent showing that a stretch-then-undo cascade exposes TSM artifacts. It is a coding pipeline, not an experimental control. There is no ASR, no per-arm measurement and no bias analysis. It is useful for a one-line citation that round-trip TSM artifacts are known. I could not open the Makhoul 1986 abstract (IEEE page not fetchable).

candidates.t: CLEESE: An open-source audio-transformation toolbox for data-driven experiments in speech and music cognition
candidates.v: J. J. Burred, E. Ponsot, L. Goupil, M. Liuni, J.-J. Aucouturier, 2019, PLoS ONE
candidates.why: Background. Tuttosi et al. 2026 (cited) used CLEESE for its local speech-rate manipulations in Study 1, so the closest cited human-perception work relies on an uncontrolled phase vocoder for local stretching. That supports the motivation for C2. It does not pre-empt anything.

candidates.t: Extreme Audio Time Stretching Using Neural Synthesis
candidates.v: L. Fierro, A. Wright, V. Valimaki, M. Hamalainen, 2022, arXiv 2211.16992
candidates.why: Background supporting the observation that artifacts grow with stretch factor k (the paper uses k=4 and 6). The material is environmental sounds, not speech, and there is no ASR or local vs global comparison.

sweeps.summary:
Short answer from the duration-probing angle: yes, the direction is new, with one wording caveat. Nothing found runs C1's core design: human speech, targeted vowel lengthening vs uniform slowing with added duration matched exactly, a sweep over k, and a check for stretcher artifacts. Nothing found touches C3 (the phase-vocoder bias tracking the artifact imbalance between arms).

The caveat is the two Tuttosi papers the paper already cites. Both tested Whisper on synthetic TTS speech and saw the same direction as C1. In the 2025 SSW paper (Whisper-medium), full-phrase WER was 24.5% with targeted lengthening, 19.4% with global slowing and 21.4% at baseline. In the 2026 paper (Study 3c), global slowing improved WER most, while the targeted model barely beat baseline. Neither matched total added duration (the 2025 design is not even ratio-matched: 1.6x on targets vs 1.2x everywhere), neither used human voices or a stretch sweep, and neither ran significance tests for the ASR results. The paper's wording, 'addressed only indirectly', does not say they already saw this direction. Stating it, and resting the novelty on exact duration matching, human voices, larger k, the artifact round-trip check and exposure control, would stop a reviewer from reading C1's direction as already known.

Mujtaba NAACL 2024 (cited) already measured WER after synthetic local prolongations on human LibriSpeech, but it has no uniform-slowing control. Xiong ICASSP 2019 (not cited) is an older phone-level tempo-modification paper in the same family as El Hajal 2025; it is optional to cite.

The probing literature (SSL layer probes, prosodic ABX, emphasis residuals, rate-normalization or phonetic-categorization studies with wav2vec2, and time-warp integration windows) looks at representations or at global stretching only. None of it compares matched local and global lengthening by WER. I found no paper probing Japanese, Finnish, Estonian or Arabic vowel-length contrasts in Whisper, wav2vec2 or HuBERT with controlled duration edits.

Coverage limits: the WebSearch budget ran out partway through, so the later queries went through the arXiv API, OpenAlex (including citation trails) and direct fetches. Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429 and DBLP was unreachable. ISCA Archive full texts were not searched directly beyond what search engines indexed.

candidates.t: You Sound a Little Tense: L2 Tailored Clear TTS Using Durational Vowel Properties
candidates.v: P. Tuttosi et al., 2025, ISCA SSW (arXiv 2506.23367)
candidates.why: Already reports the same direction as C1 for Whisper: targeted vowel/word lengthening gives higher WER than global slowing, and even higher than no slowing. Misses what is essential to C1: synthetic TTS voice rather than human speech, added duration NOT matched (1.6x on targets vs 1.2x everywhere, so the paper's label 'ratio-matched' does not fit this 2025 design), a single model, no significance test, no stretch-factor sweep, no TSM, so no artifact control. Pre-empts more than the paper credits: the paper describes the design ('compared them with ratio-matched uniform slowing', 'addressed only indirectly') but never says these studies already found the same direction for Whisper. Suggest writing that they did, and resting novelty on exact duration matching, human voices, the k sweep, artifact control and exposure control. Note that TTS duration control has no TSM artifacts, so this result also indirectly supports C1 not being purely an artifact effect.

candidates.t: Covertly improving intelligibility with data-driven adaptations of speech timing
candidates.v: P. Tuttosi, A. Lim, H. H. Yeung, Y. Wang, J.-J. Aucouturier, 2026, arXiv 2603.30032
candidates.why: A second precedent for the C1 direction on Whisper: at equal local stretch ratio (1.2x), global slowing helps the ASR more than targeted slowing. Still synthetic TTS, ratio-matched rather than matched on total added duration (global adds much more time), one model, mild stretch only (no k in {2,4,6}), no TSM artifact check, no exposure control. The paper cites it for the design but not for its Whisper result. Crediting that result explicitly would be safer than leaving 'addressed only indirectly', because a reviewer who knows Study 3c may read C1's direction as already observed.

candidates.t: Lost in Transcription: Identifying and Quantifying the Accuracy Biases of Automatic Speech Recognition Systems Against Disfluent Speech
candidates.v: D. Mujtaba et al., 2024, NAACL
candidates.why: Already shows that aligned local lengthening of human LibriSpeech recordings raises WER in modern ASR, which is one ingredient of C1. It has no global-slowing arm, no duration matching, no stretch-engine artifact check, and targets word onsets, not vowel nuclei. The paper cites it only as evidence that stuttered speech contains prolonged segments. Consider one clause saying it already measured WER under synthetic local prolongation on human speech, but without a matched uniform-slowing control.

candidates.t: Phonetic Analysis of Dysarthric Speech Tempo and Applications to Robust Personalised Dysarthric Speech Recognition
candidates.v: F. Xiong, J. Barker, H. Christensen, 2019, ICASSP
candidates.why: Weak partial: an early case of segment-specific (vowel-focused) lengthening of real speech evaluated by ASR, which is the same family as El Hajal 2025 that the paper already cites. It does not compare concentrated vs uniform lengthening at equal added duration, works in the feature domain (so no TSM artifacts), uses HMM-era systems, and aims at augmentation or normalization, not robustness probing. Optional citation next to El Hajal. Not a threat to novelty.

candidates.t: Understanding Adaptive, Multiscale Temporal Integration in Deep Speech Recognition Systems
candidates.v: M. Keshishian, S. Norman-Haignere, N. Mesgarani, 2021, NeurIPS
candidates.why: Background only: a time-warping invariance analysis of ASR models under GLOBAL stretching, with no local lengthening, no WER contrast, and no artifact control. It could motivate why uniform slowing is easier than concentrated lengthening (a model whose windows track structure duration can absorb uniform rate changes), but it tests nothing like C1 or C3.

candidates.t: Emphasis Sensitivity in Speech Representations
candidates.v: S. Cassini, T. Hain, A. Ragni, 2025, IEEE ASRU (arXiv 2508.11566)
candidates.why: Probes how natural word lengthening under emphasis is encoded in representations. It uses no synthetic duration manipulation, no local-vs-global comparison and no WER. Relevant background for the 'stress and lengthening in model representations' strand only.

candidates.t: Prosodic ABX: A Language-Agnostic Method for Measuring Prosodic Contrast in Speech Representations
candidates.v: H. Sun, S. McIntosh, K. Choi, E. Yeo, D. Saito, N. Minematsu, 2026, arXiv 2604.02102 (submitted to Interspeech 2026)
candidates.why: The closest 'probing SSL models on prosodic/length-type contrasts' work found. It does not cover vowel length, apply duration manipulation, or measure ASR WER. No overlap with C1 to C5.

candidates.t: Which words are hard to recognize? Prosodic, lexical, and disfluency factors that increase speech recognition error rates
candidates.v: S. Goldwater, D. Jurafsky, C. D. Manning, 2010, Speech Communication 52(3)
candidates.why: Correlational evidence from natural speech that locally lengthened words are misrecognized more, in HMM systems. No controlled manipulation and no duration-matched global comparison. Possible motivation citation only.

sweeps.summary: Quranic-domain answer: nothing pre-empts C1 or C4. Across about 30 queries (web, arXiv API, ISCA/ACL/IEEE-oriented; Semantic Scholar API rate-limited), no Quranic or Arabic ASR work compares lengthening targeted madd nuclei with uniform slowing at matched added duration, sweeps stretch factor, or uses any TSM artifact control. No work reports ASR WER stratified by recitation style (hadr/tadwir/tahqiq or murattal/mujawwad), so even the natural counterpart of C1 is unmeasured. Tajweed literature (QPS phonetizer, IqraEval, QuranMB, HMM duration classifiers, Yeou 2003) treats madd as a pronunciation-assessment target, not as a controlled ASR stressor; Abdelfattah et al. 2025 locate madd from text (a shared ingredient) and use global TimeStretch only as augmentation. For C4, EveryAyah leakage is recognized (Grigoryan et al. 2025 found verse-text overlap across reciters and filtered it; Quran-Lab's 2026 benchmark excludes seen reciters), but every prior work handles exposure by exclusion. None trains matched models with none/voices/exact-recording exposure, measures an exposure effect on a robustness contrast, or runs a stretch-based label-only membership probe on Quranic data. Recommendation: cite Grigoryan et al. 2025 (and optionally the Quran-Lab benchmark) as prior acknowledgement of EveryAyah overlap, which strengthens C4's motivation without threatening it; optionally cite Abdelfattah et al. 2025 for text-derived madd. Caveats: the MDPI Alshboul et al. full text was blocked, so its Maad-error remark is snippet-level; Google Scholar was not queried directly.

candidates.t: Open Automatic Speech Recognition Models for Classical and Modern Standard Arabic
candidates.v: Grigoryan, Karpov, Albasiri, Lavrukhin, Ginsburg (NVIDIA), 2025, arXiv 2507.13977
candidates.why: Acknowledges EveryAyah text overlap and handles it by filtering. It does not manipulate exposure (none vs voices vs exact recordings), does not measure an exposure effect on any robustness contrast, and has no membership probe. Background only, but it is the most citable prior statement of EveryAyah leakage and would strengthen C4's motivation.

candidates.t: Quran-Lab quranic-asr-benchmark (leakage-free Quranic ASR benchmark, 600 clips)
candidates.v: Quran-Lab, 2026, Hugging Face dataset card (v1.1)
candidates.why: Same concern (reciter-level exposure inflates Quranic ASR scores) but solved by exclusion, with no controlled exposure arms, no exposure-effect measurement, no stretching. Not peer reviewed. Useful as community evidence that EveryAyah exposure is a recognized problem.

candidates.t: Automatic Pronunciation Error Detection and Correction of the Holy Quran's Learners Using Deep Learning
candidates.v: Abdelfattah, Khalil, Abbas, 2025, arXiv 2509.00094
candidates.why: Shares one ingredient of C1's method (locating madd from text) and uses global time stretching as augmentation, but never compares local madd lengthening with global slowing, never matches added duration, and never evaluates ASR WER under targeted stretching. Tempo robustness is not evaluated by style. Could be cited as an alternative text-based madd locator.

candidates.t: Enhanced Neural Speech Recognition of Quranic Recitations via a Large Audio Model

sweeps.summary: Answer to the user's question for this angle: nothing found does C4 or C5. Across 24 queries (arXiv, ISCA, IEEE and ACL snippets, Semantic Scholar-style searches, 2010 to 2026 with focus on 2022 to 2026), no paper retrains matched ASR models on one recipe at graded exposure (none, the speakers' voices, the exact recordings) to test whether a perturbation-response contrast comes from memorization. No speech paper uses a pre-registered, hashed protocol with confirmatory tests on new speakers either. Four works share parts of C4. (1) Wang, Thakkar and Mathews 2023, plus the Interspeech 2024 follow-up: synthetic 4x sped-up canaries inserted into training, with CER-based exposure as a memorization signal. This is the closest precedent for a time-scale-based membership probe. It is not cited and should be, but it does not pre-empt C4: its setting is different and its result goes the other way (memorization detected for inserted canaries vs AUC about 0.5 for natural recordings). (2) Tseng et al. 2025: matched LLMs trained with and without text contamination, which produced only subtle WER differences. That is design precedent and also a caution. (3) Dong, Lin and Lee, Interspeech 2026: separates voice from text via resynthesis and shows that MIA AUC on speech data is confounded by distribution shift unless blind baselines are used. This bears directly on how to report the AUC about 0.5 claim. (4) Akeret 2026: training on the test set shows Whisper WER inflated by memorization. Two items are background with no threat: the Quran-Lab leakage-free benchmark (Aug 2026), which independently confirms that the EveryAyah test split overlaps most Quranic ASR training sets and so supports the need for C4; and the Miao, Shah and Teixeira MI line for ASR. Choquette-Choo 2021, which the paper already cites, already covers the generic idea of augmentation-robustness label-only MI, so the stretching probe is an application, not a new method. Suggested fixes: cite Wang 2023 and Dong 2026, add a blind baseline or distribution-match check for the membership AUC, and note per-speaker variation (Shah 2021) when reporting a pooled null.

candidates.why: Shares the key ingredient of C4's probe: time-scale-modified audio plus transcription accuracy as a membership/memorization signal. Misses what makes C4 distinct: its canaries are synthetic, compressed 4x and deliberately inserted and repeated, whereas C4 lengthens natural human recordings of evaluated speakers, uses graded exposure (none / voices / exact recordings) with matched retrained models, and asks whether exposure explains a local-vs-global contrast. Does not pre-empt C4's result (it finds memorization for canaries; C4 finds AUC about 0.5 for natural recordings), but the paper should cite it when claiming a stretching-based membership probe, and can use it to explain why its probe fails (natural stretched speech is in-distribution enough to generalize).

candidates.t: Evaluation of LLMs in Speech is Often Flawed: Test Set Contamination in Large Language Models for Speech Recognition

candidates.why: Same design logic as C4 (train matched models that did or did not see the test material, then compare), and its outcome pattern (small WER effect, detectable elsewhere) is the kind of result C4 must rule out. verified.title: AIx Speed: Playback Speed Optimization Using Listening Comprehension of Speech Recognition Models (Kawamura and Rekimoto, AHs '23, arXiv 2403.02938)
verified.human_or_synthetic_speech: Human speech only. LibriSpeech read English (native) and UME-ERJ (English read by 202 Japanese learners). The pilot also used 140 MTurk human listeners transcribing 15 LibriSpeech sentences at 0.25x to 2.0x. No synthetic TTS voice.
verified.duration_matched_global_control: Only approximately, and not by duration. The uniform baseline is played at the non-uniform output's arithmetic mean rate (1.30x LibriSpeech, 1.29x UME-ERJ). The speed loss averages per-segment rates over "specified equal intervals" of input, so matching mean rate does not match total duration: by Jensen the non-uniform output is at least as long as the constant-rate one, which gives the non-uniform arm extra time. The paper reports no output durations. All manipulations are speed-UP (the loss rewards higher rate). Global SLOWING appears only in the pilot (0.25x to 0.75x uniform, wav2vec2 WER rises while human WER/CER barely changes), with no local-slowing counterpart.
verified.artifact_control: None. The TSM/speed-change method is not named. The authors note that concatenating segments at different speeds adds noise and degrades quality, and they run voice separation on the combined output before recognition. As described this happens only in the non-uniform pipeline, so the two arms are processed differently. No stretch-and-restore round-trip, no per-arm artifact measurement, no engine comparison.
verified.models_and_languages: English only. One wav2vec2-based CTC recognizer, trained jointly with the rate adjuster (shared encoder, trained on LibriSpeech train-clean-100 plus UME-ERJ) and also used as the evaluator. So the ASR scores the allocation it helped choose, and the evaluation split is not clearly held out. The pilot used a stock wav2vec2 ASR plus humans. No Whisper, no Arabic, no multi-model comparison, no exposure or membership analysis, no pre-registration.
overlaps_partly: C1 (design ingredient only): non-uniform vs uniform time-scaling of human speech at a matched average rate, scored by ASR WER on LibriSpeech. The direction is opposite: speed-up, with an ASR-chosen allocation that by construction hurts ASR less than uniform (WER 12.96 vs 14.58 on LibriSpeech, 53.13 vs 63.90 on UME-ERJ). No lengthening, no vowel or linguistic targeting, no stretch-factor sweep, and the match is by mean rate, not duration.

C1 (global arm only): the pilot already shows uniform slowing raises wav2vec2 WER on LibriSpeech while human transcription barely changes (15 sentences, one model). So 'global slowing hurts ASR' is not new; only the local-vs-global contrast is.
verified.short_quote: the playback speed optimized by AIx Speed has lower values for both CER and WER
verified.what_paper_must_do: Cite AIx Speed as the closest human-speech precedent for comparing non-uniform with uniform time-scaling at a matched average rate using ASR WER. Credit its pilot for showing that uniform slowing raises wav2vec2 WER while human listeners barely change. Scope C1 explicitly to lengthening targeted vowel nuclei, not to non-uniform allocation in general: AIx Speed shows that an allocation the ASR itself chooses (speed-up) hurts WER less than uniform scaling, so where the time goes decides the sign. If the paper does not already have one, a random-position or non-vowel local arm at the same added duration would show that vowel targeting, not non-uniformity alone, drives the gap. Two differences are worth stating in a sentence as strengths of this design: AIx Speed matches mean rate, not total duration (so its non-uniform arm gets extra time), and it has no artifact control (only the non-uniform arm is separation-processed, and the TSM engine is unnamed). Both are exactly what C1's exact duration match and C2's round-trip check address. C2 to C5 have no counterpart here.

verified.title: Natural fast speech is perceived as faster than linearly time-compressed speech (E. Reinisch, 2016, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics 78:1203-1217)
verified.human_or_synthetic_speech: Human speech: one female native German speaker read one carrier sentence at normal rate and fast (with reductions and deletions). Target word bahnen/bannen spliced in, with a 9-step /a/-/a:/ vowel-duration continuum made by Praat PSOLA. Judged by human listeners (12 per experiment). No ASR.
verified.duration_matched_global_control: Yes, but for a different contrast. The normal-rate sentence was linearly PSOLA-compressed to the length of the natural fast sentence (about 1.38 s), and the natural fast sentence was linearly expanded to the normal-rate length (about 1.92 s). This fully crosses Duration (long/short) with fast-speech Processes (present/absent). So "natural non-uniform timing" is compared with "linear uniform scaling" at matched total duration. There is no arm that lengthens targeted vowels. The non-uniform version is a natural production that also differs segmentally (6 fewer realized segments), not a controlled local stretch of the same signal.
verified.artifact_control: One sentence in Methods: to account for artifact differences between expansion and compression, the two unmanipulated original sentences were PSOLA-resynthesized (sped up, then slowed down again) so all four versions went through manipulation. This is a stretch-and-restore round trip at unchanged duration, used only to equalize processing across conditions. Artifact damage is never measured, per arm or otherwise. The paper does not test whether the round trip actually equals the one-way manipulation. Only one engine is used (Praat PSOLA), there is no engine comparison, and nothing claims or shows that TSM artifacts bias the experimental contrast.
verified.models_and_languages: No ASR or neural models. Human listeners in a phonetic categorization task (Exp. 1) and an explicit rate comparison (Exp. 2). German only (/a/-/a:/ duration contrast). Single TSM tool: Praat PSOLA.
overlaps_partly: C2: prior use of a TSM round trip at unchanged duration (speed up, then slow down) as an artifact control. In Reinisch it only equalizes processing across human-perception conditions. It is never used to measure artifact-only damage, never split per local/global arm, never applied to ASR WER, and never compared across engines (PSOLA only). C2's measurement, per-arm, engine-bias and engine-validation parts stay new.

C1 (weak, background only): compares non-uniform (natural fast) timing with linear uniform time scaling at matched total duration and finds they are perceived differently. But the target is human rate perception, not ASR error. The non-uniform arm is natural production with deletions, not targeted vowel lengthening, and there is no stretch-factor sweep. It does not pre-empt the Local-vs-Global WER finding.
verified.short_quote: original sentences were also resynthesized (speeded up and slowed down again)
verified.what_paper_must_do:
Direct answer to the user: this paper does not do the submission's core work. It has no ASR, no targeted vowel lengthening, no per-arm artifact measurement and no engine comparison. It does use the stretch-and-restore idea itself, so the submission must not claim to have invented the round trip.

1. Cite Reinisch 2016 in the C2 method paragraph as prior use of a TSM round trip at unchanged duration. There it was a processing-equalization control in speech perception (Praat PSOLA, human listeners).
2. Frame C2's novelty as turning the round trip into a quantitative measurement. It measures artifact-only WER damage, separately for the Local and Global arms, for ASR models. It compares engines and shows librosa's phase vocoder biases the contrast while Rubber Band R3 passes.
3. Optionally note the implicit assumption in Reinisch's control. Equalizing by round trip assumes round-trip damage matches one-way damage and is the same across conditions. C2 tests exactly this, and C3 shows an imbalance between arms predicts the size of the bias.
4. Optionally cite it in related work on C1 as human-perception evidence that non-uniform vs linear timing at matched duration is not equivalent. Stress that it tests rate perception with natural reductions, not ASR robustness to targeted vowel lengthening.
5. Avoid any wording like "first to use a stretch-and-restore control".

verified.title: Talker intelligibility and listening effort with temporally modified speech (Paulus, Hazan, Adank, Interspeech 2019)
verified.human_or_synthetic_speech: Human speech. 192 IEEE sentences from two male Southern British English talkers (T08, 3.52 syll/s; T13, 4.33 syll/s), recorded in an anechoic room. Stimuli heard by human listeners (16 in Exp 1, 24 in Exp 2) in speech-modulated noise or a 10-channel noise vocoder. No ASR anywhere in the paper.
verified.duration_matched_global_control: No. The local arm ("Align") warps each talker onto the other talker's timing with VocALign, so T08 is sped up and T13 slowed by roughly the ratio of their rates (about 1.23x). The global arms are fixed WSOLA factors: Fast (x2, duration -50%) and Slow (x0.66, duration about +52%). Local and global arms therefore differ in duration, direction and magnitude, and there is no global control matched to the local arm's added duration. The local manipulation is whole-sentence nonuniform alignment to another talker, not lengthening of a few targeted vowel nuclei.
verified.artifact_control: None beyond inspection: items were "manually checked for signal processing artefacts". Each arm uses a different engine (VocALign for local, WSOLA for global), so engine and manipulation are confounded. No round-trip (stretch and restore) test, no objective TSM quality measure, no per-arm artifact estimate. In the Discussion and Conclusion the authors guess that the larger pupil response for aligned speech may come from temporal or spectral distortion introduced by the processing, but they do not test this.
verified.models_and_languages: No ASR or neural models. English only (British English talkers and listeners). Outcomes: keyword recall, SRT at 50% (adaptive, Exp 2), peak pupil dilation. Analysis used linear mixed-effects models.
overlaps_partly: C1 (tangential only): compares local (nonuniform) against global retiming of natural human speech, but the judges are human listeners, not ASR. Durations are not matched, the local arm is alignment to another talker rather than targeted vowel lengthening, and nothing is swept over a stretch factor. Cooke & Aubanel 2017, already cited, is the closer precedent for this framing.

C2/C3 (motivation only): gives a published example of the confound C2 diagnoses, with a different engine per arm (VocALign vs WSOLA) and artifacts checked only by ear. The authors themselves suggest the local processing added distortion. There is no measurement, no round-trip test, and no link between an artifact imbalance and the size of the contrast.
verified.short_quote: All items were manually checked for signal processing artefacts.
verified.what_paper_must_do: Nothing is required for novelty, since this paper pre-empts none of C1 to C5. It is a human-perception pupillometry study with no ASR, no duration matching, no targeted-vowel manipulation, no artifact measurement and no exposure control. Two optional steps: (1) cite it next to Cooke & Aubanel 2017 as human-listener precedent for comparing local and global retiming of natural speech, and as a concrete example of the arm-specific engine confound (VocALign vs WSOLA, manual artifact checks only) that C2's round-trip check is built to remove; (2) avoid any wording like "first comparison of local vs global retiming of human speech". Scope the novelty claim to ASR, exact duration matching and per-arm TSM artifact control. For the user's question: this paper does not show the direction was done before.
